_comment: Copy this to settings.json in Apps/SensorLab/ on the watch's USB volume.
Every field is optional; a missing or blank one keeps the documented
default. An out-of-range value is REFUSED, not clamped, and the refusal is
logged with the value and the range -- see Software/Libs/Header/Settings.hpp.
The app never writes this file back.
schema must be 1 exactly. A file with an unknown schema falls back
entirely rather than guessing at rearranged keys.

_comment_request: What a soak ASKS the sensors for. What they deliver is the whole point of
layer 6, and on this device the two are known to differ: 5000 ms of
requested latency produced 195 ms batches, and a requested 40 ms period
produced ~48 Hz (SleepLab ledger rows S17 and S3).
These defaults are deliberately the same numbers SleepLab asked for, so
the first SensorLab soak is a check on those measurements rather than a
new and incomparable one. 0 for either asks the driver for its default,
which is a different experiment worth running separately.
_comment_cadence: How often a soak writes one interval row per subscribed sensor, and one
per field. At a dozen subscribed types a minute is ~12 stream rows and up
to 76 value rows, roughly 12 KB -- against the Sleep Probe's measured
74 KiB for a whole night at one row a minute. Range 5..3600.
_comment_caps: Both caps, because the two failure modes differ: a long run fills the
volume slowly and a misconfigured interval fills it fast. 0 minutes means
run until stopped -- which is not the default, because an unattended run
still going three days later has stopped being a measurement of anything.
_comment_subscribe: subscribe_all on is the honest default and also the most invasive one.
Measuring a sensor changes it: subscribing costs power and IPC, and a dt
distribution taken while eleven other streams are running is NOT the same
measurement as one taken alone. Both are worth having -- the run manifest
records which -- but a first profile wants coverage.
To get an uncontended measurement of one sensor, turn subscribe_all off
and name it. only_type accepts hex ('0x10') or the enumerator name
('ACCELEROMETER'). With subscribe_all off and only_type absent the run
subscribes nothing, which measures what the service itself costs -- a
valid and occasionally useful run, and the app logs a warning so it is
_comment_fields: Layer 5: per-field min/max/mean, quantisation step, non-finite count,
stuck-run length, distinct enum values. A handful of adds and compares
per field per sample. Turning it off is how a timing-only run avoids that
cost being part of what it measures.
_comment_firmware: A FALLBACK ONLY, used when the kernel does not answer RequestSystemInfo.
The profile's primary key is normally read from the device; when it comes
from here instead, the manifest records firmware_read_from_kernel: false
and the report says so. A declared version is better than none -- a
profile with no version cannot be diffed at all -- but presenting one as
read would put somebody's memory into the field every comparison keys on.
_comment_registers: Tier 5: read sensor configuration registers directly over I2C. OFF by
default, READ-ONLY for ever, and NOT IMPLEMENTED in this build -- the flag
is parsed and recorded in the manifest so a profile can state the tier was
Apps on this device run with no isolation (MPU disabled, CPU privileged,
TrustZone off) and FwDump already demonstrates direct hardware access, so
this is possible. It would turn the accelerometer's configured range and
ODR from a layer-5 inference into a CONFIRMED fact. It would also, if it
ever wrote, reconfigure a sensor under the kernel's own driver -- and the
failure would look like a sensor fault rather than like this app.
There is no write path anywhere in this codebase, which is a stronger
guarantee than a flag. And Docs/EXPECTED.md shows the layer-5 inference is
precise enough to name the register value it implies (ACC_RANGE = 0x02,
